title: Staging, DNS, and the week before launch
excerpt: A website launch DNS checklist is unglamorous on purpose: a staging URL, a content freeze, DNS with a written rollback, and a person watching the first hour.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall. The string between screens fits a piece about the sequence that connects staging to the real domain.
caption: Launch week is a sequence, not a mood. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should happen before DNS changes?
faqs.answer: The new site should already be finished on a staging URL. Content should be frozen, or every late edit should go to staging and be checked there. Titles, forms, and the primary path should be clicked on a phone. DNS is the last step, not the moment you discover the headline is wrong.

faqs.question: How do you roll back a DNS change?
faqs.answer: Write down the previous records before you edit them. Shorten the cache time ahead of the switch so a reversal does not wait on a long-lived record. Know who can edit DNS, and keep that person available during the change. A rollback you have not written down is a theory.

faqs.question: Who watches the first hour?
faqs.answer: A person who can reach the host, the DNS, and the inbox the site writes to. They open the public URL on a phone off the office network, submit the form, and watch for a certificate error, a redirect loop, or a message that arrives nowhere. A launch without a watcher is how small failures become a day.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A website launch DNS checklist is short because the week is not a design review. You already have a site. The job is to point the real name at it without losing the ability to go back. The sequence is a staging URL, a content freeze, DNS with a written rollback, and a person watching the first hour. Skip one of those and the launch becomes a debugging session in public.

Treat the list as the plan for the week, not as a mood. Launches feel ceremonial. The failures are clerical. A record pointed at the wrong host. A form that still posts to staging. A certificate that was never issued for the name people actually type.

## A staging URL that is the real site

Staging is the new site on a hostname you can load before DNS changes. It uses the same build you intend to ship. It is not a screenshot and not a design prototype. Click through it as a stranger. Homepage, the path to contact, the form, the footer links, a page you know regulars will open.

Do this on a phone, on a connection that is not the office wifi. [web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) is the reference for what you are watching. A good Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds, a good Interaction to Next Paint is 200 milliseconds or less, and a good Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.1 or less, judged seriously rather than on the single best load. Staging will not reproduce every visitor's phone. It will show you a hero image that is enormous, a font that blocks the headline, and a button that jumps when a banner arrives. Fix those before the name points here. After DNS, every fix is a fix on the live company.

Check the title of each important page against the page itself. Google's guidance on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) says each page needs a descriptive title element, distinct from the others, and that vague or boilerplate titles serve people badly. Staging is when you read them. A title that still says the old offer, or that says Home on every URL, will be what search results and browser tabs show once the domain moves.

## A content freeze

Pick a moment when the words stop changing, at least on the pages in the launch. A freeze is how staging and production stay the same thing. Without it, someone edits the headline in a doc, the site ships the previous sentence, and the argument about which is official happens after customers have seen both.

Urgent corrections still happen. They happen on staging, they get checked, and then they ride the same build. They do not happen as a quiet edit on production that nobody told the person watching DNS. One path for changes. Write it in the channel so the freeze is a shared fact.

The freeze includes third parties. A script, a font, a chat widget, an analytics tag. Adding one on launch morning is a favorite way to make a tested site slower than the site you tested. If it was not on staging, it is not in the launch.

## DNS, written down

Before you change anything, copy the current records somewhere outside the DNS host. The apex, the www name, any mail records, and anything else you do not fully understand. Mail is the usual casualty. A site launch that breaks the inbox is a worse outage than a late homepage, because the company goes quiet while the new design looks fine.

Know which records the new host needs, and change only those. Leave mail alone unless a person who runs mail is on the call. Shorten the time those records are cached before the day of the switch, so a mistake can be reversed without waiting out a long memory in the world's resolvers. Put the time back to a calmer value once the new site has been steady. There is no magic minute count that fits every registrar. There is a requirement that you know the number you set, and that you do not first discover it during the emergency.

Issue the certificate for the names you will serve, including both the apex and www if you use both. Decide which one is canonical and redirect the other. A loop, or a warning in the browser, is the failure mode to provoke on staging with a hosts-file test if you can. Finding it from a customer's screenshot is the expensive version.

Write the rollback as a sentence you could hand to a tired person. Restore these records. Here is the previous deployment, and here is who can promote it. If the sentence names a login you cannot open, you do not have a rollback. You have a favor to ask.

## The first hour

Name one watcher. They are available from the moment DNS changes until the new site has been seen from outside the office. They load the public URL on a phone that is not logged into the company's tools. They look for the certificate, the right homepage, the redirect from the other hostname, and the form.

They submit the form and confirm the message arrived in the inbox you think it did. They click the primary action. They open a page that used to exist and confirm it still does, or that it redirects on purpose. They watch the error log if you have one. They do not spend the hour admiring the type.

If something is wrong and the rollback is cleaner than a forward fix, they roll back. Pride is a bad incident commander. A reverted DNS record and a calm note to the team is a successful rescue. An hour of improvising on the live domain, while mail may also be confused, is how a small miss becomes a story.

Tell the people who answer customers that the change is happening, and tell them when it is done. They will get the first confused replies. They should know whether to apologize for a transition or to treat a complaint as a real bug.

## The day after

Look again in the morning, from a network you did not use yesterday. Caches lie overnight and then tell the truth. Check mail. Check the form. Check that the host bill and the domain are in accounts you own, so the launch did not also hand the keys away.

Then lift the freeze on purpose. Edits resume through the same path you tested. The launch is over when the watcher has nothing to watch, not when the announcement post goes up.

The wider list, including copy, links, and the inbox, sits beside this one. [A checklist before you publish a company site](/blog/checklist-before-publishing-a-company-site) is the next piece if the week before DNS still has open questions about the page itself.
